claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 during elevated-temperature gas exposure is governed by the formation or absence of a protective oxide scale.
In oxidizing gases, Cr, Al, and Ti selectively oxidize.
Selective oxidation produces a thin, adherent oxide scale.
The oxide scale limits further degradation.
The protective scale preserves the underlying fcc matrix.
In reducing gases, failure or breakdown of the scale causes localized elemental depletion.
Scale failure in reducing gases causes microstructural damage.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has a fine-grained, intact fcc matrix.
The starting alloy exhibits high strength and fatigue performance.
The relevant structural mediator is a stable surface oxide scale enriched in Cr, Al, and Ti.
An adherent oxide scale retards oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Absence or instability of the scale facilitates localized depletion at locations such as grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a continuous, thin protective scale and minimal internal degradation.
Reducing exposure will produce no sustained oxide scale or evidence of scale breakdown.
Reducing exposure will cause more localized degradation, grain-boundary weakening, and microstructural damage than the starting-state baseline.
Responses outside the intended temperature or gas-composition boundaries may be intermediate or mixed.
Oxide-formation kinetics and degradation rates may vary with processing history and subtle compositional gradients.
Similar scale formation and degradation under oxidizing and reducing exposures, or a lack of correlation between scale state and degradation, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
